what: Hess Midstream owns the pipes, processing plants and storage that move oil, gas and water around the Bakken shale in North Dakota. It does not own the oil; it charges fees for gathering, processing and transporting what its customers produce, under long-term contracts with minimum volume commitments.
customers: Principally the Bakken production business formerly operated by Hess and now part of Chevron, which accounts for the great majority of volumes, plus some third-party producers in the same area.
money: Fee-based gathering of crude oil, natural gas and produced water from well sites.
Gas processing, fractionation and crude terminalling and storage.
Rail and pipeline loading facilities moving Bakken barrels to market.
moat: The infrastructure is physically connected to specific wells, so the producer has no practical alternative once the pipes are in the ground. The contracts carry minimum volume commitments, which means Hess Midstream is paid whether or not the oil flows, and new gathering systems in the Bakken are both expensive and unnecessary given the existing network. This is about as close to a toll road as energy gets.
risks: Nearly all volumes come from one customer. Chevron’s capital allocation decisions about Bakken drilling determine this company’s growth entirely.
Debt of about $3.8B against essentially no cash, at $1.9M, is very high relative to a $6.2B market value, which is normal for midstream but leaves the distribution exposed to refinancing costs.
Minimum volume commitments protect revenue only until they are renegotiated, and the renewal terms are the key uncertainty.
Bakken production has been broadly flat for years, so volume growth requires Chevron to commit new capital to a basin it acquired rather than built.
Seven analysts average a $32.29 target, only about 8% above the current price, so limited upside is expected.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year shown, from $1.2B in 2021 to $1.6B in 2025, and the contract structure makes it predictable.
Free cash flow of $901.1M against a $6.2B market value is a very large yield, and it supports a high distribution which is the main reason to hold this type of security.
Fee-based contracts with minimum commitments mean the business is insulated from the oil price in a way producers are not.
Chevron’s ownership arguably strengthens the counterparty: the credit quality behind the contracts is now much better than it was.
The shares trade at about 6.9 times free cash flow and 8.0 times EV/EBITDA.
watch: Chevron’s stated Bakken drilling plans, and the terms of contract renewals. This is a toll road whose traffic is decided by one customer, so what that customer intends matters more than anything in the financial statements.
view: Midstream energy is the closest thing the market offers to owning a toll road, and Hess Midstream is a particularly pure example. It owns the gathering lines, processing plants and terminals that Bakken oil and gas physically have to pass through, charges a fee per barrel, and is paid under long-term contracts with minimum volume commitments — meaning it gets paid whether the oil flows or not. The oil price, which dominates everything for a producer, is largely irrelevant here. What matters is volumes and contract terms.

The attraction is the cash. $901 million of free cash flow against a $6.2 billion market value, at 6.9 times free cash flow and 8.0 times EV/EBITDA, funding a large distribution. For an income-oriented investor that is a legitimate proposition and the contract structure makes it considerably more reliable than it looks from the sector it sits in. The $3.8 billion of debt against essentially no cash looks alarming to anyone unfamiliar with midstream, but infrastructure financed against contracted cash flows is the normal shape of these businesses, not a warning sign in itself.

The risk is concentration, and it is the entire analysis. Almost all of the volume comes from one producer, and that producer is now Chevron following the Hess acquisition. This cuts two ways. The counterparty credit is now far stronger than it was — being paid by Chevron is better than being paid by a mid-cap independent. But the growth decision has moved to a company that did not build this basin and has the entire Permian, Kazakhstan, Guyana and the Gulf of Mexico competing for the same capital. Bakken production has been broadly flat for years. If Chevron decides the Bakken is a cash harvest rather than a growth asset, Hess Midstream’s volumes do not grow, and a toll road with flat traffic is a bond rather than an equity.

That is why the seven analysts see only 8% upside and why I think they are roughly right. The distribution is well covered and the contracts protect it; the question is whether there is anything beyond it. Minimum volume commitments also eventually come up for renewal, and the negotiating position of a counterparty that is now one of the largest oil companies in the world is better than the one Hess had. I would own this for the yield with clear eyes about the growth, and I would read Chevron’s capital allocation statements more carefully than Hess Midstream’s own disclosures.
bull: Chevron commits capital to Bakken drilling, volumes grow through infrastructure that is already built, and a well-covered high distribution rises on top of a 6.9 times free cash flow multiple.
bear: Chevron treats the Bakken as a harvest asset, volumes stay flat, and renewal negotiations with a far stronger counterparty compress the fees that fund the distribution.
